section_1.title: The Failure of Euclidean Dimensions
section_1.content: Introduce the standard dimensions (0D point, 1D line, 2D plane, 3D cube) and demonstrate how they fail to describe complex, 'rough' natural shapes like coastlines or clouds.
section_1.example: Compare a smooth circle (2D) to a jagged, self-similar cloud boundary; the cloud has more 'filling' power than a line but less than a plane.

section_2.title: The Scaling Law: Prerequisite Knowledge
section_2.content: Explain the relationship: if you scale a shape by factor 's', its size increases by 'N = s^D'. Solve for D: D = log(N) / log(s). This is our bridge from integer to fractal dimensions.
section_2.example: A 1D line segment doubled (s=2) results in 2 copies (N=2). log(2)/log(2) = 1. A 2D square doubled (s=2) results in 4 copies (N=4). log(4)/log(2) = 2.

section_3.title: Calculating the Fractal Dimension: The Koch Snowflake
section_3.content: Apply the formula to the Koch Snowflake. Visualize replacing 1 line segment with 4 smaller segments that are each 1/3 the original length. Calculate D = log(4)/log(3) ≈ 1.26.
section_3.example: An animated sequence showing a 'Robot Architect' recursively adding triangular 'tentacles' to a line, showing how the length goes to infinity while occupying a space between 1D and 2D.

section_4.title: Real-World Applications & Synthesis
section_4.content: Connect fractal dimension to surface area efficiency in nature. High fractal dimension implies more surface area packed into limited space, essential for biological function.
section_4.example: Visualize a 'Deep Sea Creature' (e.g., a coral reef) using its high fractal dimension to maximize oxygen absorption from water compared to a smooth, flat surface.
